Abstract
A method is described for the identification of astaxanthin glucoside esters from snow alga *Chlamydomonas nivalis* by means of liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry with atmospheric pressure chemical ionization. Liquid chromatography was performed using a reversed-phase column packed with porous silica particles and eluted with a mobile phase consisting of acetonitrile with 0.1% formic acid at a flow rate of 0.2 mL/min. The mass spectrometer used electrospray ionization in both positive and negative modes to determine molecular formulae of unknown compounds. Based on this data, two glucoside ester forms of astaxanthin were identified. The method provides reliable results and can be employed for further studies of the snow algal species *C. nivalis*.

Background: Leprosy is a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae which affects the skin, peripheral nerves, mucous membranes, and eyes. Drug resistance is a serious problem for leprosy control. It is important to assess drug resistance because it can affect the outcome of the treatment. There has not been enough research on drug resistance in leprosy, especially primary resistance.

Abstract: Skin biopsy homogenates obtained from three cases of lepromatous leprosy with no prior history of antileprosy treatment were tested in the mouse footpad for the sensitivity of M. leprae to multiple drugs. Nine M. leprae strains, obtained by subcutaneous inoculation of these biopsies into mouse footpads, were isolated. Of these, five strains showed resistance to dapsone (D), rifampicin (R) or clofazimine (C), and 2 strains showed resistance to the combination D/C/R, indicating that primary resistance can occur with either single drug or multiple drugs at the same time. The other 2 strains were susceptible to all the above 3 drugs. The data suggest that primary resistance can be found even in lepromatous leprosy patients, who have never taken any antileprosy drugs. The results are important to prevent failure of the standard multidrug therapy.

**Abstract**

Currently, traditional family values that have been passed down through generations appear to be at risk. This has significant implications for the stability and health of individuals, families, and communities. This paper explores selected issues related to the intergenerational transmission of family values. The focus is on understanding how the transmission of values can occur from one generation to the next; it also discusses how the transmission can be affected by various factors such as age, sex, education, and culture. A review of literature was conducted to obtain information about the subject; articles and books were read from different cultures including the United States, China, India, Brazil, Australia, and the United Kingdom. We also considered the role of education, religion and culture in transmitting values. Finally, we discuss how these transmission processes might be better understood and improved.

generations.raw_text: As a member of the testis-specific serine/threonine protein kinase (TSSK) family, Tssk4 is exclusively expressed in the testis and plays an essential role in male fertility. We previously reported that Tssk4 forms a complex with Odf2, the sperm specific protein, and is required for mouse spermatogenesis and male fertility. In this study, we have determined that Tssk4 can directly phosphorylate Odf2 at Ser-76 through an in vitro kinase assay. Moreover, the in vivo experiments using a conditional knockout of Tssk4 indicate that the Ser-76 of Odf2 is critical for the interaction between Tssk4 and Odf2, which is also important for mouse male fertility. These results suggest that Tssk4 plays a critical role in spermatogenesis by regulating the function of Odf2. Further research on this topic may provide useful information for future clinical diagnosis and treatment of infertility.

The case of a young female patient with acute symmetrical ascending polyneuropathy as a manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus is reported. There was involvement of several cranial nerves and the cerebrospinal fluid showed increased protein concentration. The patient presented to the hospital with symptoms that included generalized muscle weakness, dysphagia, and double vision. The patient also had a history of Raynaud's phenomenon, arthritis, oral ulcers, hair loss, photosensitivity, and pleurisy. Based on these symptoms, and after performing serologic tests, the diagnosis of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) was confirmed. The patient had never been treated for SLE before, and during her hospitalization, she received plasma exchange therapy, intravenous immunoglobulins, methylprednisolone, pyridostigmine and plasmapheresis. She improved clinically during this hospitalization and was discharged with the plan to follow up in the outpatient clinic.
The patient presented with Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) as a manifestation of SLE. To the best of our knowledge, GBS is not a usual manifestation of SLE, thus reporting this case is useful as it may help in the future to identify patients who may be suffering from both SLE and GBS.

The photon decay of the relativistic Coulomb excitation of the double Giant Dipole Resonance (GDR) in the target has been observed in 1 AGeV 209Bi on 208Pb. The photon spectrometer used is a Germanium gamma-ray array. The experiment was done at the GSI Helmholtzzentrum für Schwerionenforschung. The results reveal that the GDR is a composite state and has a dipole character. It is also shown that the 2-phonon component contributes a significant fraction to the double GDR, which agrees with theoretical model. The experimental data and the analysis results show that the double GDR has a strong coupling to the particle states and that it can be used as a tool to investigate the structure of the 208Pb.
